lines.text: Bigger chargers don't hurt your phone.
So why doesn't a big laptop charger overload a small phone?
Apple says an iPhone can use a higher wattage USB C adapter, even your Mac laptop's.
That works because phone and charger agree on power first, using USB Power Delivery, so the phone takes only what it can handle.
And bigger can be faster: a new iPhone seventeen charges to half in about twenty minutes on forty watts or more.
The real danger is heat. Apple warns that above thirty five degrees, a battery can lose capacity for good.
Any good USB C charger is fine; if your phone gets hot while charging, take off its case.

post.title: Can a bigger charger hurt your phone?
post.caption:
Myth: a bigger charger hurts your phone 🔌

Apple says you can charge an iPhone with a higher-wattage USB-C adapter, even the one from your Mac laptop. Phone and charger agree on power first (USB Power Delivery), so the phone only takes what it can handle. Bigger can be faster: an iPhone 17 gets to 50% in about 20 minutes on a 40 W adapter or more.
The real danger is heat: Apple warns that above 35 °C (95 °F) a battery can lose capacity for good.

Any good USB-C charger is fine; if your phone gets hot while charging, take off its case. Send this to the friend who keeps three chargers "just in case".

Photo: the Sun by NASA/SDO (public domain).

sources.note: Apple, Charge and connect with the USB-C connector on your iPhone: a power adapter that complies with the USB-C standard, "This includes USB Power Delivery"; "If you have a 20W USB-C power adapter or higher-wattage USB-C power adapter, like the one that came with your Mac laptop, you can use it with your iPhone" (read 14 Nov 2026).

Apple, Fast charge your iPhone: "You can fast charge iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, and iPhone 17 Pro Max up to 50 percent battery in around 20 minutes with a 40W adapter or higher"; adapters that support USB Power Delivery (USB-PD) (read 14 Nov 2026).

Apple, Batteries, Maximizing performance: "avoid exposing your device to ambient temperatures higher than 95 F (35 C), which can permanently damage battery capacity"; "Charging the device in high ambient temperatures can damage it further"; "If you notice that your device gets hot when you charge it, take it out of its case first" (read 14 Nov 2026).

holds: the verdict rests on screen after the last word (the charger and phone stay lit, pulses running) so it can be read and saved
